title: Is Christianity a White Man's Religion?
excerpt: The charge is stronger than its usual answer: the cross did reach most of the world on the same ships as the chains. But the faith was Asian and African before Europe had heard of it, and the people it was used against kept it and judged their masters by it.
body:
A young man comes home from his first year at college and tells his grandmother, as gently as he can, that the Jesus she has prayed to all her life is the god of the people who owned her great-grandparents. On the wall behind her hangs the picture that has always hung there, a pale man with light brown hair and blue eyes. In another town a man who has gone to church for fifty years has never once asked what the people in his Bible looked like, because in every picture he was shown they looked like him. And a history student, who believes none of it, has read enough to state the case plainly: the cross came to most of the world on the same ships as the chains.

The charge that Christianity is a white man's religion is usually answered too fast. Someone points out that Jesus was not European, as though that settled it. The charge is better than that, and it should be heard in full.

## The Charge

It is not mainly a claim about where the faith began. It is a claim about what arrived. Christianity reached the Americas, most of Africa south of the Sahara and much of Asia in the company of European conquest. Men who bought and sold human beings had them baptized and taught them a religion with the dangerous parts removed. Missionaries who gave their lives for the people they served very often treated European dress, names and manners as part of the gospel. In the 1880s Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a freed slave who had become the first African bishop in the Anglican church and had led the translation of the Bible into Yoruba, watched younger Englishmen take his mission apart around him. When he died, his successor was white. The lesson, as this site's history course puts it, was that Africans could be converts but never leaders.

Frederick Douglass saw the American form of it from the inside and wrote it down in 1845: "We have men-stealers for ministers, women-whippers for missionaries, and cradle-plunderers for church members." For centuries the churches of Europe and America painted Christ as one of themselves, and then carried the picture around the world.

A religion, the argument runs, is what it does. For four hundred years this one gave its sanction to the theft of continents and taught the robbed to be patient. Whatever it was in the beginning, it became the faith of the people with the ships, and a person of African or Asian or native descent who holds it now is holding his conqueror's creed.

The facts in that argument are true, and the church has no right to hurry past them. An [earlier essay](/writing/what-the-church-got-wrong-about-race) sets out what American pulpits did with the Bible, and none of it is softened here. The question is whether the conclusion follows. To answer that, the history has to be taken from the start, and it has to include what Christians of color themselves did with the faith.

## Where It Was Born

Jesus was a Jew from Galilee, in western Asia. As a small child he was carried into Africa, where his family lived as refugees until the king who wanted him dead had died (Matthew 2:14–15). When he was too weak to carry his cross, the soldiers seized a passerby to carry it for him: "Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country" (Mark 15:21). Cyrene was a city in North Africa.

The book of Acts tells how the faith spread, and its map is worth reading slowly. On the day of Pentecost the crowd that first heard the apostles is listed by homeland: "Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia," people from the lands that are now Iran and Iraq, then Asia Minor, then "Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene," then Arabia (Acts 2:9–11). The only Europeans in the list are islanders from Crete and "visitors from Rome."

In the eighth chapter an angel sends the evangelist Philip to a desert road, where he meets "an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure" (Acts 8:27). He is the finance minister of an African kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt, riding home in his own chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah. Philip explains the passage to him, he asks to be baptized at the first water they come to, and he "went on his way rejoicing" (Acts 8:39). Luke tells this story before he tells the story of any European coming to faith.

The first church that preached to non-Jews in any numbers was at Antioch in Syria, and Luke says who began it: "men of Cyprus and Cyrene" (Acts 11:20). It was at Antioch that "the disciples were first called Christians" (Acts 11:26). When Luke lists that church's leaders, two of the five are "Simeon who was called Niger," a nickname that is the Latin word for black, and "Lucius of Cyrene" (Acts 13:1). These are the men who laid their hands on Paul and sent him out as a missionary.

Only after that does the gospel cross into Europe, and the way Luke tells it is striking. Paul sees a vision in the night of a man from Macedonia begging, "Come over to Macedonia and help us" (Acts 16:9). Europe enters the Christian story as the place that needs help.

## The First Thousand Years

The centuries that followed kept the same shape. The first great Christian writer in Latin, Tertullian, wrote in Carthage, in what is now Tunisia. The young mother Perpetua kept her prison diary there before she died in the arena in 203. Cyprian, the city's bishop, was beheaded in 258. In Egypt around 270 a farmer named Antony walked into the desert, and from his example grew the monastic movement that would later copy the Bible through Europe's dark centuries. Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria from 328, was exiled five times for insisting that the Son is truly God, and the creed that most churches on earth still recite owes a great deal to his refusal to move. Augustine, whose account of grace both Catholics and Protestants claim, was born in North Africa, served as bishop of an African port and died there. This site's history course calls North Africa "for centuries the theological engine room of the whole church." The doctrines by which a Christian in any country knows who Christ is were, to a remarkable degree, worked out by Africans.

South of Egypt the story is as old. The church historian Socrates, writing in the fifth century, tells of a young man named Frumentius who was taken captive to a distant kingdom, rose to manage its affairs and gathered the Christians he found there. He went to Alexandria to ask for a bishop, and Athanasius "requested Frumentius himself to accept the bishopric." The kingdom was Aksum, in Ethiopia, and the story has an unusual confirmation. Athanasius preserves a letter in which the Roman emperor Constantius writes to the rulers of Aksum, "Aezanes and Sazanes," demanding that they send "Frumentius, Bishop of Auxumis" to Egypt to be examined. The emperor wanted an African church brought into line with his own theology, and in the middle of the fourth century he had to ask. That church has not ceased to exist since.

To the east the faith spoke Syriac, a form of the Aramaic that Jesus spoke, and it reached India early enough that the Thomas Christians there count among the ancient churches.

Europe north of the Alps came late. Patrick went to the Irish in the middle of the fifth century. The king of the Franks was baptized around 496. The mission to the English began in 597, and the old story about its origin is that a Roman churchman had seen fair-haired English boys for sale in a slave market. Boniface carried the faith into the German forests in the eighth century. When William Carey argued in 1792 that Englishmen should take the gospel overseas, he reminded them that the first missionaries had once come to "the barbarous Germans and Gauls, and still more barbarous Britons." For most of the church's first millennium the people now called white were the mission field, and some of them were the slaves.

One caution belongs here. The ancient world did not sort people by color as the modern world learned to. Nobody thought to record what Augustine or Athanasius looked like, and it would repeat the old mistake in reverse to draft them into a modern race. They were Africans, and that much is plain. The idea that a faith could belong to a complexion would have meant nothing to them.

## How It Came to Look White

Two things changed the picture. The first was a loss. From the seventh century on, the lands where the church had been strongest, Syria, Egypt and North Africa, came under Muslim rule, and over the following centuries their churches shrank to minorities or vanished. North Africa, the home of Augustine, has held only a remnant of Christians for more than a thousand years. The ancient churches of Egypt, Ethiopia and India lived on, mostly out of Europe's sight. Europeans mistook where the church had survived for what the church was.

The second was conquest. When Europe's ships went out, the faith went with them, and so did the trade in human beings. This site's history course says of the nineteenth century that it "moved on imperial rails." Some missionaries fought the empire's crimes and some approved them. The theology bent with the money. Christians who needed slavery found it in Genesis, and Christians who needed colonies found a duty to civilize. We painted the Lord with our own face and sent the picture out with the missionaries. In our own country we would not kneel beside the people we had baptized.

That is the church's sin, and "we" is the right word for it. The churches that did these things were not impostors wearing the church's name. They held the creeds and loved their Bibles, and they did this anyway. The charge says that the faith became the servant of one people's power, and for several centuries, across much of the world, it was.

## Who Carried It

The charge leaves out the people it speaks for. They were handed a religion edited to keep them quiet, and they read the rest of the book.

Enslaved men and women in America heard the story of Israel brought out of Egypt and understood that it was about them. In the Bible that was being used against them they found a Christ their masters had not preached. Douglass, who wrote that line about men-stealers, wrote this in the same paragraph: "I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ: I therefore hate the corrupt, slaveholding, women-whipping, cradle-plundering, partial and hypocritical Christianity of this land." He had every reason to throw the whole thing back, and what he did was judge the slaveholder's religion by Christ. It is hard to call that a conquered mind. To say that such people simply swallowed their captors' religion is its own kind of contempt, and it comes oddly from anyone who claims to respect them.

The same thing happened wherever the Bible was translated. A missionary who put the Scriptures into a people's own language had told them, whatever else he believed, that God spoke their tongue. Most of the actual preaching across Africa and Asia was done by local believers whose names the sending churches never learned. As this site's history course has it, "They were the engine."

And the numbers moved. By the estimates that course gives, about ten million Africans were Christians in 1900 and more than three hundred million by the century's end. Around 1980, for the first time since the Middle Ages, most of the world's Christians were not Europeans or North Americans. Some of the largest congregations in Europe's capital cities are now led by African pastors. None of this makes the churches of the global south a finished thing. They have their own false teachers and their own temptations. But it does mean that the phrase "white man's religion" describes one stretch of the story, some four or five centuries of it, as it looked from inside the empires. It was not true before that, and it is not true now.

## What the Faith Says About Itself

History can show that the charge is too small. It cannot show that the faith is true, and a skeptic is right to say so. The harder question is whether the capture was a betrayal of Christianity or an expression of it, and that has to be answered from its own book.

At Pentecost the first thing the Spirit did was make the gospel heard in the languages of the listeners. The church was given no sacred language and no holy culture that every convert must adopt. Its first great argument was over this very point. The earliest believers were Jews, and some of them held that Gentiles who came to Christ must take on the customs of the people who had brought them the message. The apostles ruled that they need not (Acts 15:19). When Peter later drew back from eating with Gentile believers, Paul "opposed him to his face" (Galatians 2:11). The principle was settled in the church's first generation: the culture of the messenger is no part of the message. Every missionary who made converts dress and worship like Englishmen was breaking the church's oldest ruling.

Paul states the result in a list that takes in the far north: "Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11). And the Bible's last vision of the redeemed does not show the differences erased. John sees "a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages" (Revelation 7:9), and later he sees the kings of the earth bringing "the glory and the honor of the nations" into the city of God (Revelation 21:24, 26). The nations are still there, and each has brought something.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess that God made every nation "from one man" (Acts 17:26), that Christ died and rose for people of every tribe and language, and that his church is one body. To rank human beings by race, or to treat one people's customs as the gospel, contradicts that confession. It was sin when the church did it with a clear conscience, and it is sin now.

What repair requires of churches that profited from this history is a question on which faithful Christians give different answers, and the earlier essay sets two of them side by side without choosing.

Whether Christianity is true is another matter, and the faith's history, shameful or glorious, cannot decide it. That rests on whether Jesus rose from the dead.

The grandmother's picture is wrong, and it should come down. But the grandson is mistaken about whose faith she has been keeping. It was carried to Europe from Africa and Asia, and the churches of Europe and America are the daughters of churches in Antioch, Alexandria and Carthage. We forgot that for a few centuries and behaved as though the house were ours. Two of the men who laid hands on the first missionary to Europe were a man called Black and a man from Africa. In the crowd John saw, the children of the northern barbarians will be standing where they always stood, among the nations that were sent for late.

*"Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God."* (Psalm 68:31)

*"Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all."* (Colossians 3:11)
